AI Adoption at the World Bank Group

Evidence from the AI-Enabled Research Bootcamp Baseline Survey

Executive summary

  • AI is already part of everyday work: 98% use it for their job and 68% of time-use respondents report at least one hour per day.
  • Widespread use has not yet translated into broad adoption of advanced workflows: only 24% have tried a coding agent, 26% have created a memory file, and 27% have used someone else's reusable skill.
  • AI is already helping respondents produce more and better work: 65% report producing more output, 66% higher-quality outputs, and 45% spending less time on analysis. These are self-reported benefits, not measured productivity gains.

These are self-reported baseline findings from bootcamp survey respondents, not measured impacts or a representative sample of WBG staff. Percentages use non-missing answers to each question; multi-select percentages need not sum to 100%. Tool use is ever-use for work; task use covers the last four weeks.

Module 1: Current Use of Generative AI

  • AI use is already widespread and intensive: 98% use it for work; among the 62 answering the time-use question, 68% report at least one hour per day.
  • Chat and office tools dominate, while coding agents remain less common: among the 62 tool-question respondents, 100% have used mAI, 84% MS Copilot, and 81% third-party chat tools, compared with 24% who have used a coding agent.
  • Writing and knowledge work lead recent use: Documents (85%), Background Research (82%), Email (69%) are the most common tasks; 48% also use AI for data analysis and visualization.
  • AI-assisted work reaches outputs, but detailed disclosure is uncommon: 65% have had such work included in an output. Among those 40 answering the disclosure question, 28% gave detailed disclosure, 38% mentioned AI without details, and 28% wanted to disclose but were unsure how.

Module 2: AI Workflows, Impact & Verification

  • Memory files and reusable skills are not yet mainstream: 26% have created a memory file and 27% have used someone else's reusable skill; 50% and 37%, respectively, do not know what these are.
  • Respondents report both quality and productivity benefits: 66% say AI helps them produce higher-quality outputs, 65% more output, and 47% more in-depth work. These are self-reported benefits, not measured impacts.
  • Reproducibility gains are less evident: only 18% report improvement, while 45% report no change and 31% are unsure.
  • Verification relies primarily on manual review: 77% manually review all outputs, compared with 34% using benchmarks and 23% using automated tests or QA checks.

Module 3: GitHub, Copilot & Safe AI Use

  • GitHub-based workflows are not yet widely adopted: 22% currently use GitHub for version control, while 38% are unfamiliar with it.
  • Active WBG Copilot use is limited: 10% are active users and another 13% have a license and are exploring; 69% have heard of it but never used it, or do not know what it is.
  • Safe-use responses are split: 41% selected working with raw data in mAI/M365 Copilot, 41% selected synthetic-data-assisted script development with local execution, and 17% were unsure.

Module 4: Background & Expectations

  • Participants bring substantial WBG experience: 67% have worked at the WBG for 5–19 years.
  • Expectations are strongly practical: 94% want tools they can apply to their jobs and 86% greater productivity; improving work quality (79%) and technical skills (79%) are also priorities.
  • Extensive AI use coexists with limited formal preparation and self-rated expertise: 75% have not taken an AI-for-research course; 40% rate their knowledge poor/very poor, 46% average, and only 14% good/excellent.
